Main_Finding: Tendon stiffness and neuromuscular function undergo significant changes during adolescence, influenced by age, sex, and physical activity levels. Tendon stiffness increases initially due to material property changes and later through cross-sectional area enlargement. Male adolescents exhibit higher tendon stiffness than females, which may contribute to sex-based differences in injury susceptibility. Neuromuscular function improves with maturation, though voluntary activation remains lower in children compared to adults.
Practical_Application: Coaches should prioritize the use of mixed designs when feasible to capture both cross-sectional comparisons and longitudinal trajectories. Ensuring adequate sample sizes, particularly for diverse populations, is essential for robust findings. Regular training and calibration of measurement tools are recommended to maintain high levels of reliability and validity. Start with simple weekly structure, prioritize completion, and progress only after stable adherence and recovery.
Low_Resource_Applicability: Coaches can apply these findings by tracking developmental milestones through visual assessments and adjusting training intensity based on perceived effort and recovery status. Simple tools like goniometers can help monitor joint range of motion and flexibility, supporting safe progression of neuromuscular exercises. Prioritize consistency, easy riding, and RPE-based step-wise progression before adding harder work.

Title: Sex Differences in Youth Athletic Development
Authors: A. Sargsyan; Sargsyan, A.; Ashot Sargsyan; Ford et al.
Main_Finding: Adolescent athletes, particularly males between 13–15 years old, experience increased injury risk during peak height velocity due to rapid bone growth outpacing muscle, tendon, and neuromuscular adaptation. Overuse injuries are prevalent, influenced by high training volumes, low recovery, early specialization, and multi-team participation.
Practical_Application: Allow athletes to participate in multiple sports during early stages. Periodize training to focus on different sports. Develop transferable skills. Monitor training loads and recovery signs. Implement recovery strategies like sleep, reload weeks, and nutrition. Foster psychological recovery by giving athletes freedom and fun. Start with simple weekly structure, prioritize completion, and progress only after stable adherence and recovery.
Low_Resource_Applicability: Coaches can use simple methods such as tracking height changes, observing changes in coordination and movement efficiency, and implementing recovery strategies like ensuring sufficient sleep and active recovery without needing advanced equipment or testing. Practical_Application: Coaches should consider implementing either TP or BP models, focusing on a balanced distribution of low-, moderate-, and high-intensity training sessions. Incorporating short blocks of moderate-intensity threshold (MIT) and high-intensity interval (HIT) training is recommended to simulate race-specific efforts. Start with simple weekly structure, prioritize completion, and progress only after stable adherence and recovery.
Low_Resource_Applicability: Coaches without access to advanced monitoring tools can apply these findings by using perceived exertion (RPE) scales to guide training intensity distribution. Wellness scores and subjective fatigue ratings can help adjust training load in response to feedback. Prioritize consistency, easy riding, and RPE-based step-wise progression before adding harder work.

Main_Finding: Physical inactivity, diet, and stress are significant risk factors for cardiovascular diseases (CHD). Modifiable risk factors include obesity, high blood pressure, and high serum cholesterol, while nonmodifiable factors include age, gender, and heredity. Insulin resistance, often linked to obesity and poor diet, plays a central role in metabolic syndrome, increasing the risk of hypertension and type 2 diabetes.
Practical_Application: Implement a progressive jogging program starting with 10-second jogging intervals and gradually increasing to continuous jogging. Incorporate dynamic warm-ups and cool-downs. Monitor heart rate to ensure adherence to the target heart rate (THR) zone. Encourage participation in group activities but emphasize skill matching to prevent imbalances. Start with simple weekly structure, prioritize completion, and progress only after stable adherence and recovery.
Low_Resource_Applicability: Encourage walking, household chores, and community-based activities for older adults without access to specialized equipment. Suggest prenatal yoga and swimming for pregnant women. Promote school-based physical education and access to calcium-rich foods for adolescents. Prioritize consistency, easy riding, and RPE-based step-wise progression before adding harder work.
